newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - French bank boss "hostage" in siege.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - French bank boss "hostage" in siege.

text.p: The chairman of French bank Credit Foncier declared himself a hostage on Monday and broke off talks with trade unions as a staff siege at the troubled bank's headquarters dragged into a fourth day.
"He now considers himself hostage," a union official told Reuters. "The unions have decided to continue the occupation. But this is all being done in full respect for those involved."

Several hundred staff at the 145-year-old home loans group spent the weekend at the downtown Paris headquarters in a peaceful occupation which started on Friday in a last-ditch bid to halt government plans to shut the bank down.

Chairman Jerome Meyssonnier, who had insisted until late on Sunday evening that he understood the anguish of the protestors, changed tack on Monday and called Finance Minister Jean Arthuis by telephone to say negotiations with staff were being halted.
"He told me this morning that he could not keep the dialogue going as long as he was denied freedom of movement," Arthuis told Europe 1 radio.
Arthuis, who interrupted a weekend break in western France to meet unions at the Paris offices on Saturday, insisted that the government was not willing to bail Credit Foncier out.
"The state does not want to become a shareholder of another state bank," he said.

Unions said close to 1,000 employees were now involved after several hundred, many accompanied by their children, spent the weekend in the vast marble hall of the bank's headquarters on a diet mostly of sandwiches and coffee.
The unions, which are battling for public sympathy and to keep a bank with 3,300 staff alive, said Credit Foncier branches had nevertheless opened for business as usual on Monday morning.

The atmosphere inside the bank over the weekend was more like that of a church picnic than an armed camp. Meyssonnier, sporting jeans and a jumper rather than traditional banker's suit, had warned against dramatising his plight.
"They haven't cut my finger off yet," he quipped at a news conference he gave in the boardroom on Sunday evening.

Two national trade union leaders turned up over the weekend in a show of support for staff. A union offical said Marc Blondel, the pugnacious leader of the Workers Force (Force Ouvriere) union could make an appearance there later on Monday.

Meyssonnier, who has been held along with other members of the board since around midday on Friday, made it clear he was looking for another solution to the break-up of Credit Foncier and still believed the group could make as much as a billion francs in profit this year.

The plan, hatched by Arthuis in July after Credit Foncier announced a loss of nearly 11 billion French francs ($2 billion) for 1995, would see 1,500 staff and the group's portfolio of low-cost housing loans taken over by the cooperatively-run Credit Immobilier.
The rest of the bank, one of France's oldest, would be wound down, raising the spectre of heavy job losses.

Mayssonnier said he was trying to test the possibility of a "common project" with Credit Immobilier, an indication that he may be looking for some form of merger or joint venture which would keep Credit Foncier intact.

The standoff is shaping up as a new test for the government of Prime Minister Alain Juppe, after bowing to union protests in the past, most recently when it agreed in December to allow striking truckers to retire at 55 years of age instead of 60.

The saga also highlights close ties between the state and the banking sector, as staff and shareholders suspected an effort to sink the bank and close an embarrassing saga of losses in which the state was involved. ($1=5.409 French Franc)
